etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Latin analogia, from Ancient Greek ἀναλογίᾱ (analogíā), from ἀνα- (ana-) + λόγος (lógos, “speech, reckoning”).

definitions.definition: A relationship of resemblance or equivalence between two situations, people, or objects, especially when used as a basis for explanation or extrapolation.

quote.citation: 1841, Ralph Waldo Emerson, chapter 6, in Essays: First Series:
quote.text: Yet the systole and diastole of the heart are not without their analogy in the ebb and flow of love.

quote.citation: 1869, Charles Dickens, chapter 18, in The Uncommercial Traveller:
quote.text: Is there any analogy, in certain constitutions, between keeping an umbrella up, and keeping the spirits up?

quote.citation: 1901, Edith Wharton, chapter 12, in The Valley of Decision:
quote.text: The old analogy likening the human mind to an imperfect mirror, which modifies the images it reflects, occurred more than once to Odo.

quote.citation: 1983 January 3, “How to Write Programs”, in Time:
quote.text: Perhaps the easiest way to think of it is in terms of a simple analogy: hardware is to software as a television set is to the shows that appear on it.

quote.citation: 2002, Harlan Coben, Gone for Good‎[1], →ISBN, page 75:
quote.text: A kid living on the street is a bit like — and please pardon the analogy here — a weed.

definitions.definition: (geometry) The proportion or the equality of ratios.

(grammar) The correspondence of a word or phrase with the genius of a language, as learned from the manner in which its words and phrases are ordinarily formed; similarity of derivative or inflectional processes.
